extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook guidance and exercises about properties of morphisms of schemes: fibers (generic/general/geometric), preservation under base change, generically finite/finite, geometric connectedness/irreducibility/reducedness/integrality, universal injectivity (radicial), and the Segre embedding for products of projective schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms have finite fibres
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite morphisms have finite fibres. (See Remark 9.3.4 and Exercise 7.3.K.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you haven’t done Exercise 7.3.K showing finite morphisms have finite fibres, now is a good time; this is straightforward given the surrounding material. (Used as a basic test/property when checking finiteness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic fibre behavior depends on base point/residue field
rubrics_metrics.description: Fibres of a morphism may vary in scheme-theoretic structure depending on the point (e.g., preimage of 0 vs -1 vs the generic point can produce different residue-field behaviours and field extensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: preimage of 0 may have special nilpotent behavior; preimage of −1 or the generic point can lead to a field extension of degree 2. Try to draw pictures (e.g., parabola picture) to internalize possible fiber phenomena. See Example 9.3.3 and Exercise 9.3.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up at a point: description and exceptional divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: The blow-up Bl(0,0) A^2_k ⊂ A^2_k ×_k P^1_k is cut out by the single equation xv = yu; the fibre over each closed point of P^1_k is an isomorphism away from (0,0), while the fibre over (0,0) is an effective Cartier divisor called the exceptional divisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Bl(0,0)A^2_k as parametrizing ordered pairs (point p, line ℓ) with p and (0,0) on ℓ. The blow-up is a surgery that removes a point and glues in a P^1, giving another smooth surface in this example. This example generalizes to A^n_k (see Exercise 9.3.F and Chapter 22).

rubrics_metrics.name: General fibre vs generic fibre
rubrics_metrics.description: General fibre: there exists a dense open U ⊂ Y such that fibres above any point in U have the property; Generic fibre: Y is irreducible and refers to the fibre over the generic point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General implies generic, but not conversely in general. Under good hypotheses (Y irreducible and Noetherian, π finite type), properties that hold/ fail for the generic fibre (e.g., emptiness) extend to the general fibre by Chevalley’s Theorem 7.4.2 or Exercise 7.4.L. Use this when passing from a generic fiber statement to an open neighborhood statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generically finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is finite type, π is generically finite if π is finite after base change to the generic point of each irreducible component (equivalently the preimage of the generic point of each irreducible component of Y is a finite set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion can be defined more generally (see Stacks tag 073A). Exercises (e.g., 9.3.G) show that for π : X → Y affine finite type generically finite with Y reduced, there is an open neighbourhood of each generic point over which π is actually finite — use reduction to affine case and monic polynomials for generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely presented morphisms are locally pullbacks of nice families
rubrics_metrics.description: Finitely presented families (morphisms) are locally pullbacks of particularly nice families: any finitely presented morphism is locally (on the base) a pullback of a finite type morphism to a Noetherian scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.3.H constructs a base change diagram Spec B ← Spec Z[x1,...,xN] making the morphism a pullback of a finitely presented π'. Thus results proved for Noetherian schemes and stable under base change extend to locally finitely presented morphisms; use the tensor‑finiteness arguments and the finite presentation definition in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley’s theorem for locally finitely presented morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely presented B-algebra, the image of Spec A → Spec B is a finite union of locally closed subsets; more generally, if π : X → Y is quasicompact locally finitely presented and Y quasicompact, then π(X) is a finite union of locally closed subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the affine finitely presented case using base change tricks (Exercise 9.3.H). The general form of Chevalley’s Constructibility Theorem appears in EGA/GR references for stronger formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties preserved by base change (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reasonable properties of morphisms are preserved under base change: open embedding, closed embedding, quasicompact, quasiseparated, affine morphism, finite, integral, locally of finite type, finite type, locally of finite presentation, finite presentation, quasi-finite (with care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check preservation often by reducing to affine cases and using explicit descriptions of fibre products. Exercises 9.4.B and 9.4.C enumerate these; warnings: the notion “finite fibres” need not be preserved by base change (see Exercise 9.4.C and Example 9.2.3). Use Chevalley and the tensor‑finiteness trick when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity preserved by base change; injectivity not preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Surjectivity is preserved by base change (Exercise 9.4.D). By contrast, injectivity is not preserved by base change (example Spec C → Spec R loses injectivity upon base change by Spec C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show surjectivity preserved, one may argue using tensor products and maximal ideals; for injectivity issues, see §9.4.1 and the discussion of how to 'rectify' failures via stronger notions such as universal injectivity (radicial morphisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric point and geometric fibre
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric point of X is a morphism Spec k → X where k is an algebraically closed field. A geometric fibre of X → Y is the fibre over a geometric point Spec k → Y, i.e., X ×_Y Spec k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric points enrich the notion of points (plain points, scheme-valued points, geometric points). Geometric fibres are used to define geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced fibres: require the property for all geometric fibres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrically X (connected/irreducible/integral/reduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism has geometrically connected (resp. irreducible, integral, reduced) fibres if all its geometric fibres have that property. A k-scheme X is geometrically connected (resp. irreducible, integral, reduced) if the structure morphism X → Spec k has geometrically connected (resp. ...) fibres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although checking over all algebraically closed field extensions seems daunting, in practice failures are detected after finite extensions; many equivalences (Ra–Rd, Ia–Id, Ca–Cd) reduce checking to particular field extensions (e.g., separable or perfect closures). See the 'Hard fact' 9.5.2 and subsequent propositions for precise reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences for geometrically reduced/irreducible/connected (Ra–Rd, Ia–Id, Ca–Cd)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelve statements for each property: e.g., XK is reduced for all fields K (Ra); for all algebraically closed K (Rb, geometrically reduced); for K = k (Rc); for K = k^p (Rd, perfect closure). Similar lists for irreducible (Ia–Id) and connected (Ca–Cd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial implications: (Ra)⇒(Rb)⇒(Rc) and (Ra)⇒(Rd), etc. Hard fact (9.5.2): in fact (Rd)⇒(Ra) and analogously for the other rows, so these conditions are equivalent under appropriate hypotheses. Use these equivalences to reduce verification to finitely many field extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: behavior of geometric properties via finite/separable/perfect closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures of geometric connectedness/irreducibility/reducedness can already be detected after a finite extension of fields; for many checks it suffices to base change to k, to the separable closure, or to the perfect closure depending on the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic facts about finitely generated extensions of perfect fields (Fact 9.5.16) and tensor‑finiteness tricks to reduce general field extensions to finite/separable/purely transcendental cases. See Propositions 9.5.10–9.5.20 and exercises 9.5.F–9.5.N for methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: If k is separably closed, connected ⇒ geometrically connected
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is separably closed and Y is a connected k-scheme, then Y is geometrically connected (Corollary 9.5.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses that Spec K is geometrically connected over k for any field K (Proposition 9.5.10) and Lemma 9.5.9 on bijection of connected components after base change. Apply this to deduce geometric connectedness for connected schemes over separably closed fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: If k is separably closed, irreducible ⇒ geometrically irreducible
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is separably closed, A a k-algebra with Spec A irreducible, and K/k any field extension, then Spec(A ⊗_k K) is irreducible (Proposition 9.5.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof reduces to finitely generated cases and uses images of nonempty opens and closed points to derive contradictions if reducible. Use Exercise 9.5.L and 9.5.K for related facts and the extension to general XK (Proposition 9.5.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducedness preserved under tensor with geometrically reduced algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is geometrically reduced over k and A is reduced over k, then A ⊗_k B is reduced (Proposition 9.5.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the case A finitely generated and then to a product of fields; then use the definition of geometric reducedness. Propositions 9.5.18–9.5.20 extend to field extensions of perfect fields and to schemes. Use tensor‑finiteness trick where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of varieties: conditions for affineness/irreducibility/connectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 9.5.23: (a) If k is perfect, the product of affine k-varieties is an affine k-variety. (b) If k is separably closed, the product of irreducible affine k-varieties is irreducible. (c) If k is separably closed, the product of connected affine k-varieties is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the affine case and apply earlier propositions on reducedness, irreducibility, and connectedness (Corollary 9.5.21, Exercise 9.5.K, Corollary 9.5.11). Once 'variety' is defined more generally, the adjectives 'affine' can be removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universally injective (radicial) morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is universally injective if it is injective on underlying sets after any base change. Examples: all locally closed embeddings and all monomorphisms are universally injective. This generalizes purely inseparable field extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For field extensions K/L, Spec K → Spec L is universally injective iff K/L is purely inseparable (Exercise 9.5.P). Equivalent characterizations for a morphism π : X → Y: (i) π universally injective; (ii) for every field K, Hom(Spec K, X) → Hom(Spec K, Y) is injective; (iii) π is injective and for each p, κ(p)/κ(π(p)) is purely inseparable (Exercise 9.5.Q). The notion is stable under composition, base change, products, and is local on the target (Exercise 9.5.R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Segre embedding (product of projective schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Segre morphism P^m_A ×_A P^n_A → P^{mn+m+n}_A sends ([x0,...,xm],[y0,...,yn]) to the matrix of coordinates [x_iy_j] (z_{ij}), and is a closed embedding; the image (Segre variety) is cut out by the 2×2 minors (rank 1 condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check on affine opens via explicit coordinate maps zab/ij ↦ xa/iyb/j; surjectivity of the ring map on opens shows closed embedding property. Exercise 9.6.B: show scheme-theoretically the image is defined by vanishing of all 2×2 minors. For m=n=1 this recovers the quadric surface in P^3 and its two rulings; coordinate-free descriptions via Sym•(V^∨ ⊗ W^∨) and product of Proj of graded rings are given in Exercises 9.6.C and 9.6.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor-finiteness trick for reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated proof technique: write elements as finite sums of decomposable tensors and replace rings/fields by finitely generated subrings/subextensions generated by the occurring coefficients to reduce to finitely generated or Noetherian cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout (e.g., in proofs of openness after base change Lemma 9.5.6, irreducibility/connectedness/reducedness propositions) to reduce general field/scheme extension questions to finite type situations where geometric arguments and existence of closed points can be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: 'reduced fibres' and other naive properties can fail under base change in characteristic p
rubrics_metrics.description: In characteristic p, inseparability causes failures: e.g., for k of characteristic p, k(u)/k(u^p) inseparable leads to k(u) ⊗_{k(u^p)} k(u) exhibiting nonreduced behaviour; thus reduced fibres may not be preserved under pullback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rectify by passing to geometric fibres or using the notion of geometrically reduced and use the results in §9.5 (e.g., Propositions 9.5.17–9.5.20) to control such phenomena. Exercise 9.5.A and the surrounding discussion give practical examples.
